en: 1. Oṃ Svasti! Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
Oṃ, having paid homage to one's chosen deity twice and to Vināyaka preceded by the Praṇava.
This *Gūḍhadīpikā* commentary is being composed by one named Kuśala, the son of Bālakṛṣṇa, who is the grandson of Kṣemaṅkara. 2.
Once, the son of King Śrībhoja went to another country.
From some cause... thereupon, immediately after that, Śrī Kālidāsa beheld his wife.
In the meantime, the rainy season also arrived.
Then she, whose beloved was away,
seeing the clouds, spoke these words to her friend.
The great poet, the illustrious Kālidāsa, having introduced that very same subject,
desired to describe the rainy season.
He composed a great poem (*mahākāvya*) in the *yamaka* style, titled *Ghaṭakarpara*.
Now he describes the characteristics of a woman whose beloved has gone abroad (proṣitapreyasī): "She [for whom], for some reason..."
The husband has gone to another country.
Having set a time limit,
she who has placed her hopes [in him] is considered a *proṣitapreyasī* (one whose beloved is away) [ŚT 81]. And she,
upon seeing the clouds, for six...
In verses.
First, she spoke to her friend.

15. But surely, since it has been stated that "the composition of verses (*vṛtti*) in narrative form (*sargabandha*) is indeed the definition of a *mahākāvya*," how can the *Ghaṭakharpara*, which consists of only a few verses, be a *mahā-* [kāvya]? 16. [This is the objection.]
17. The nature of poetry (kāvyatva).
Regarding this, he says: Because it is composed by great poets, and because its meaning is profound.
And because it is composed in new meters in every verse,
it possesses the status of a *mahākāvya*.
Is it not the case that it is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) that one should perform an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) at the beginning of a work, in its middle, and at its end? Therefore...

4–5. Why, immediately after the opening benediction (*maṅgalācaraṇa*), does [the author] first describe the rainy season with the words "having approached the dense sky" (*nicitaṃ kham upetya*) and so forth?
To this, he says:
Having heard the question of the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), "Indeed, for what purpose is the performance of an auspicious rite (maṅgalakaraṇa)? the opponent (vādī) says:
The performance of the auspicious rite (maṅgalakaraṇa) is for the purpose of completing the treatise preceded by the destruction of obstacles.
Therefore, [the word] "siddhā" [=].
He says: Is the completion of the book preceded by the destruction of obstacles due to auspiciousness alone, or rather from something else?
If it is the first case.
[Objection: Then, in that case, is it the rule that wherever there is an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), there is the completion of the treatise preceded by the destruction of obstacles?
Or rather, is it that wherever there is the completion of a work preceded by the destruction of obstacles,
there is auspiciousness?
In that regard, it is not the first.
The means of valid cognition.
Because, as seen in the *Kiraṇāvalī* and other works, there is no completion of the work even though an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) is present.
Since that is untenable, the second [alternative] is not [possible].
Because, although the completion of the work— such as the *Kādambarī*— is preceded by the destruction of obstacles, no auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) is manifested at its commencement;
therefore, it is not established that the auspicious rite is the cause of its completion.
As for what you said at the beginning, middle, and end of the treatise— namely, that "only an auspicious invocation (maṅgala) should be performed" [22-3],
and "for what purpose" [24], and so forth— f3.

I shall now prove that all of this is indeed your lack of authoritative status. For no wise person, having become an authority, would ever disregard the auspiciousness appropriate for the commencement of a treatise.
At the beginning of a treatise, [the salutation] is performed by the learned precisely because it was established first.
Auspiciousness is threefold: the object of homage, the exposition, and the form of benediction.
For them, the clouds performed an auspicious act by providing the very substance that covers the sky; therefore, there is no fault.
Or rather, what else?
[It is not from another], because this position has been disregarded by the poets.
It is all-pervasive,
because its arising is observed precisely through that [restraint].
However, in the first nine chapters of the *Kiraṇāvalī*, there was no completion of the work due to an abundance of obstacles and a scarcity of auspicious factors.
According to the principle that "as long as there is auspiciousness,

so long there is an absence of obstacles," and because [the work] such as the *Kādambarī* was completed outside the main text due to the performance of auspicious rites and the paucity of obstacles, it reaches its conclusion.
12. Therefore, this has resulted in nothing but a failure to refute [the position].
Now he states the very subject matter once again.
13. A woman whose beloved is away, seeing the clouds, [speaks] with six [verses].
In the verses,
it was stated at the beginning [in verse 114] that she first spoke to her friend.
The poet Tilaka of the Kula family elucidates those statements.
These words were spoken by the woman whose lover was away.
16. "Is raised" is connected with the sixth verse that follows. "What is this?"—this is connected with the second [verse], "O you whose tusks are like white water-lilies."
Thus ends the introduction.
4.1 Oṃ! Having approached the dense sky, by means of the clouds...
By the waters of those who have subdued the pride of their hearts through love,
the dust has been laid to rest.
"Even the sun and moon on earth are not perceived by her whose lover is away"— this speech is uttered by the woman separated from her beloved;
thus [it is said] in the sixth [chapter].
4. The logical connection (anvaya): "What is this?"—O you whose tusks are like white water-lilies (*kumuda*), [this] is connected with the second [verse]. 5. [End of section.]
By means of waters; by means of fluids.
On the earth, that is, on the ground, dust— that is, fine particles—
is struck down, meaning it is pacified.

Because the agent is expressed by a word ending in the third case, it is established with respect to the object expressed by a word ending in the first case; this is the action denoted by a primary derivative suffix (kṛdanta).

In the phrase "on the earth" (*kṣitau*), the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of the object (*viṣaya*). Regarding *rajaḥ*, the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *rajas* [denotes] the quality [*guṇa*], dust [*dhūli*], pollen [*parāga*], and also the menses of a woman."
Having done what was peace accomplished? Having approached— that is, having reached— the sky, which is space.
"Space is declared to be the void (kha)," according to the *Ekākṣarī*. When space is reached by clouds, then water and dust [arise].
It becomes capable of pacifying;
therefore.
It is said that one should approach the earth.
Or rather—the application of effort.
In some instances, according to the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya* that "the fifth case [is used] for the sense of the seventh," the second case is used in the sense of the fifth.
Of what kind is the sky? It is "filled with" (*nicita*) those who give water (*nīradāḥ*), hence it is "water-giving."
14. It was not covered by what kind of clouds?
For a woman who is separated from her beloved...
The earth itself is the heart;
they tear it—that is, they afflict it—with those [weapons]. *Rada* means "to scratch" or "to wound" [SV 229,8]. *Api* is used here in the sense of certainty.
The sun and the moon—those two, the sun and the moon, are not perceived; the meaning is that they have gone beyond sight, O beloved. *ī*.
18. The sense is: "At this very moment, why does he not come to me?
5.1. Thirteen words of this verse are to be understood; because it is in the form of poetry, [the word count] is not [to be taken literally].
The two [sections] are cut off; their forms are as follows:
the mantra for delusion is *chanda*;
its characteristic is that.
In the first and subsequent [feet], there are *sa*, *sa*, *ja*, and a *guru* [syllable];
*sa*, *bha*, and *ra* constitute the "Deluding Mantra" (*mohanamantraka*), followed by a *laghu* [syllable].
They also say that this very [meter] is Vaitālīya. //~//
The swans flee out of fear of the clouds; today the beginnings of night are not graced by the moon.
The peacocks, their teeth like jasmine buds, cry out at the arrival of the clouds, intoxicated by the fresh water. 2.
7. *kundasamānadantī*: the remainder [of the compound] is "by means of the buds of *kunda* flowers"; she whose teeth are similar (*samāna*) to those. 8. She who has teeth that are equal.
She; of her.
An address: "O swans, today at the arrival of the clouds!"
9. They run, they go. [The root] *dru* means "to go" [Dhātupāṭha 216, 10]. From what? From the fear of thundering clouds. [The root] *ṇad* [means "to sound"];
*vaṇa* [means] "in a distinct or indistinct sound" [Dhātupāṭha 229, 29].
Those who roar are "nadantaḥ."
Those clouds that produce indistinct sounds are "roaring clouds. From the fear arising from them— therefore.
The fifth [case ending] is used for the cause of fear. 12.
For it is well known that swans depart now with the arrival of the clouds. 13. It is not only the swans that flee.
Moreover, even the faces of the nights now, beginning from the twilight,
are not possessed of the moon.
Those in whom or those in which the moon exists— these are they.
Fifteen; the meaning is "no."
Furthermore, at this present time, O Śikhin!
The peacocks are crying out;
they are making a distinct sound.
Of what nature is it?
O Śikhin!
—Intoxicated by fresh water.
(17) That which is fresh water; by that she is intoxicated. For those who are intoxicated, the very nature of their being is the manifestation of sound. Intoxicated.
The meaning is that the virtuous utter clear words.
This is the meaning.
O you who possess union with the beloved, why should I not also be afraid of the thundering cloud, which resembles a swan?
2. Why would they not be delighted by the resemblance to peacocks? It is an undesirable encounter for the swans; it is a desirable encounter for the peacocks.
And it has been said:
"The rainy season is desired by peacocks, but for swans it is considered otherwise.
This [verse] consists of twelve words.
5. There are five [syllables in each quarter]. The meter is Indravajrā.
Its definition:
that Indravajrā consists of ta, ta, ja, and ra. Thus.
The sky, shrouded by clouds at night, does not shine; likewise, one who has abandoned the crossing does not approach Hari, who is easily served.
And now the cloud, accompanied by Indra’s weapon, thundering like elephants in a state of fury, brings about a state of agitation in those who resemble mountains. // 3 //
9. O beloved. At night, during the night, the sky is the atmosphere;
"nabhas" means the intermediate space, the firmament—thus [it is said].

10. *mara* [1.2.1]. It does not shine, it does not gleam. The root *bhā* [SV 272, 8] means "to shine. Here, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of the object (*viṣaya-artha*), namely, in this night. The word *bhāti* refers to the present tense; because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), [the locative is employed].
The agent is expressed only in the nominative case, ending in the neuter gender; and those [verbs] which are stated to be intransitive are also mentioned, such as *lajjā*.
From the root *dīp* in the sense of "shining" (dīptyartha), which is an intransitive (*akarmaka*) verbal root— what kind of sky is it? The heaven (*dyauḥ*) is covered (*āvṛta*).
14. It was covered again.
Of what kind? "Vitāram," meaning that from which or in which the stars (tārā) have departed; and furthermore, today, at the arrival of the clouds.
Sleep approaches or reaches Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
the root *i* [in the sense of] "going" is used here [as per Dhātupāṭha 276,30].
With the prefixes *abhi*, *upa*, and *upa-sarga*, this verbal root has the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*);
or rather, those roots which have the sense of "going" (*gati*).
These are the meanings of the questions.
In some places. Of what kind is Hari? He whose nature (*śīla*) it is to enjoy bliss—that is him.
The suffix *tṛn* is used in the sense of "nature" (*śīla*). [Pāṇini 3.2.134]. f7.
The meaning is "experiencing happiness";
furthermore,
today, at the arrival of the clouds, the water—
2. These two clouds bring about (āvahati) the agitation (saṃrambha), that is, the anger, of the elephants (ibhānām). [utpāda]...
3. *dayati*. With the prefix *āṅ*, it means "producing. What was he doing? Making a sound—uttering a cry. [The root] *ras* means "to sound" [Dhātupāṭha I.745].
Of what kind of elephants? Those who support the earth (*bhuvam dharanti*).
"Five mountains; resembling them, equal to them—of those [mountains]. Of what kind is the cloud?—Possessing Indra’s bow (sendrāyudha); existing together with Indra’s bow."

*Indrāyudha* is the rainbow of Śakra; thus says the *Amara-kośa* [1.2.11]. This [verse] consists of twenty syllables per quarter and is composed in the *vasantatilakā* meter. The *vasantatilakā* meter is defined by the sequence *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, *ja*, *ga*, *ga*. // 3 // // 3 //
It was bestowed upon the mountains, where the serpents were terrified by the thundering clouds and the water was struck by lightning.
The water falls with a roaring sound into the caves that are beautiful with their wondrous forms.
4 // And furthermore:
11. At this present time, water falls into the ravines and caves. [The root] *pat* is used in the sense of falling.
12. Here too, because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the action (*kriyā*) have been indicated; the agent—
And there are thirteen activities; two of them have been defined.
And those that are intransitive have been stated by the learned:

"In the sense of heating (santāpa), as well as flowing (kṣaraṇa), drying (śoṣa), and falling (patana)," and so forth; many have been mentioned, though I have shown only a few for fear of prolixity. Of what kind is the water? On the mountains (naga), that is, on the peaks (parvata) — [ta]...
16. That which is accompanied by lightning (*vidyut*) is a rain-cloud (*jalada*); [the fruit] was offered—that is, given—by that cloud.
17. In what kind of mountains?—[as indicated by the word] *svanetṛ*.
*svana* and *dhvana* mean "sound";
those which sound are called *svananta*.
Those who were afraid of the clouds— that is, the rain-clouds— making a sound.
The serpents are the possessors of coils; in those [clouds], they dwell. They are called *ambhodharas* because they bear water (*ambhas*).
[They are] the uragas.
"A serpent is called *bhogin*," according to the *Amara-kośa*.
(1.7.8) Furthermore, what kind [of sound]? A deep and resonant roar on all sides.
That which has sound as its [quality]—2—that. In what kind of caves?
That form which is wonderful,
by that [form] beautiful women are captivating of the mind— among them; or else, those whose form is wonderful.
Now, someone quickly propitiates those faces of beloved women,
which have been provoked by the agitation of passion and anger.
The thundering clouds cause longing in travelers and sorrow in those at home.
O Ananta, that [pleasure] arises within women.
// 5 // Again:
8. Seeing that his arrival was in vain, he speaks of the change in householders who are full of desire;
and with the other half [of the verse], he describes the partiality toward the clouds.
"Api" means certainly; "ka" refers to a lustful man. Now, at this present time during the rainy season, those faces of beloved women—
11. Quickly, swiftly, it inspires confidence;
it generates joy. Ṣadḷ vi[=]...
12. In the cases of taking refuge, going for protection, and despondency. [SV 246,18]
[The suffix *ka* is added] after a verbal root that takes an object when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), provided it has a meaning other than its original sense. [SV 389,26-29].
Of what nature are the faces?
"Rati" means at the time of pleasure (*rati-samaye*); "vibhrama" [is the confusion].
The fourteen *vilāsas* (graces) therein are exceedingly provoked and made crooked; because they especially cause the mind to wander, they are called *vibhrama* (bewilderment).
delusion; error; confusion.
According to the *Vaijayantī* [2.2(puṃŚ).69], it is used in the sense of doubt, delusion, and beauty;
[it refers to] clouds.
Clouds.
Resounding, making the sound "śaṅ" seventeen times.
Or rather, the reading is "santaḥ pathikān pathikam iti," meaning they cause travelers to yearn [or rejoice].
When the clouds arrive, travelers stay right where they are; therefore, there is no suffering from traveling on the road and so forth.
The sense is that they do not cause delight in warding off the [mental] wound (*kha*).
Alternatively, they cause longing;
that is, they possess longing.
They perform [their duties] while traveling on the path,
remaining entirely free from longing through their divine activity.
Furthermore, because they remain during the arrival of the clouds and because of the absence of [usual] activity,
longing arises in travelers for their homes at that time.
4. Among their wives: among the wives of those travelers; there [arises] endless, boundless sorrow.
5. It arises (*samudbhavati*);
[here] the verbal root *bhū* is used in a sense other than its primary meaning due to the two prefixes *sam* and *ud*.
Its sixteen feet are now to be known;
here too, the meter is Vasantatilakā. 5. //~//~//~//
When the mansion of the Sun is obscured, it falls from the sky into the water, producing grief.
When the God of Love and the heart were both prepared to strike, this [state] arose in one whose beloved was away.
Alternatively— Sundarī, distressed by her separation from her beloved and overcome by longing, having perceived the clouds at the onset of the rainy season,
will deliver her messages.
A woman whose lover has gone abroad; that is, the wife of a traveler who has departed on a journey.
A person is intoxicated excessively by means of improper conduct;
thus she is called a *pramadā*. By her, this speech was previously shown.
It is proclaimed and explained.
Because it is a *kulaka*, there is no fault in the repetition.
Under what condition is the expression "it makes the day of the sun" employed? It is in the sense of its manifestation, that is, in the mass of its radiance.
In that [place], which is a forest—that is, a multitude—of lights, that is, of splendors. May they be.
*Prabhā*, *ruk*, *rucis*, *tviṭ*, *bhā*, *bhās*, *chavi*, and *dyuti*—these are synonyms for "light" (*dīpti*), according to the *Amara-kośa* [1.2.35].
When it is said "being concealed" (*chādite*), the meaning is "being covered" (*channe*). Likewise, *khā* [=].

17. From the sky; [the word] *kha* [is used] for the sky, the lord of birds, and the heavens, according to the *Dharaṇī*. When he falls into the water—into what kind of water?—into that which "produces sorrow" (*śokabhāvane*). Sorrow (*śoka*) means torment (*santāpa*).
"He cultivates" or "he restrains";
alternatively, he causes grief to be cultivated, that is, he makes it manifest—
for those whose husbands are away, this is the cultivation of grief.
The suffix *yu* is applied according to the *uṇādi* rules.
2. The meaning is "in that production of grief.
Because of the presence of the *yamaka* (rhyme), there is no distinction between the two *ba*s. *Ba* = [the letter *ba*].
In the three places [of articulation], only the letter *va* should be pronounced;
such is the meaning.
And it has been said in the *Vāgbhaṭālaṃkāra*:

In the case of the syllable *ṅ*, [in *yamaka* verses and those characterized by *śleṣa* and *citra*], there is no distinction between *ba* and *va*, nor between *ḍa* and *la*. Furthermore, when what? When it is within the heart (*hṛdi*). At the end.
When Manmatha, the god of love,
was prepared to strike— that is, to cause [him] to be slain— ...
6. That which exists and churns is called *matha*.
The tormenting of the mind.

*Manmatha*: it is correct because it belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* (class of words defined by its form). Regarding that, the *Amara-kośa* states: "Madana, manmatha, and māra [are synonyms]. A *kalāpaka* consists of four [verses].
That which follows is known as the Kulaka.
In the seven [verses] composed in the Rathoddhatā meter:
"O clouds, you have come at all times;
yet now that my beloved has departed, you will surely kill me in his absence with your mercilessness, for he dwells in a foreign land. (7)
11. Thus, manifesting a reproach toward the cloud on behalf of her husband who has gone abroad, she says: 12. O Cloud! When [my] beloved...
My beloved.
Having gone to another country,
one should then, having relied upon all seasons previously— such as spring, summer, and so forth— swiftly abandon them.
"You have come," [as in] *āgatās stha* (you are come),
the second person plural ending; you—

The agent is [denoted] by the suffix -m (the *kvip* suffix); it is accepted as such because of the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*). Due to the absence of an object (*akarmakatva*), there is an absence of the object (*karmābhāva*).
16. Indeed, certainly; previously, you will kill me—that is, you will cause me to be slain—without that beloved one.
17. You will have me executed.

Since it is stated that in connection with the word *vinā*, the third and fifth cases (*tṛtīyā* and *pañcamī*) may also occasionally be employed (cf. SV 142, 22–23), the third case is used here in connection with *vinā*. Of what kind?
19. *Priyeṇa*—by one from whom *ghṛṇā*, meaning compassion (*anukampā*), has departed; that is, by such a person.
According to the *Amara-kośa*: "Kṛpā, dayā, anukampā, kāruṇya, karuṇā, and ghṛṇā are synonyms for compassion. [1.6.18]
"2. Ghṛṇā, kṛpā, and jugupsā—these are the meanings of Dharaṇī," according to the Dharaṇī [kośa]. [627]
Again.
Of what kind [is it]?
It is not a place for another, that is, for other people.
foreign lands; abroad.
He whose nature it is to serve that [teacher]— by him;
his fifteen points should also be understood.

5. "Speak quickly to that traveler who has defiled the road; for you yourselves are the ones who swiftly traverse the path. 6. Let her, whose heart is set on another land, be released today—or rather, let your wife [be released]. What is there to say? 8.
Now he speaks the message:"
O clouds!
You yourselves—tell me, speak—what is that beloved like? [He is] one who has been defiled by travelers.
Protecting travelers;
or,
that which arises on the path.
In a compound, the elision of the case-ending (*aluk*) of the first member sometimes occurs [even when it ends in a consonant], as in *pathika*.
He is both a traveler and one covered in dusty soil; he takes—that is, he grasps—him. Alternatively, he is one who takes the dust of travelers—him.
Reṇu is [the name] of two.
12. In the feminine, [the word] *dhūli*.
Dust is not [the same as] the two-fold *rajas*.
Thus says Amara [2.8.100].
Alternatively: "pathikanirdayam. Regarding "pāṃsula," Dharaṇī states: "It means 'cruel' or 'vile'."
Is it not the case that this speech should not have been addressed by a beloved wife to her husband? True; however, there is no fault, as it was spoken in anger.
Where—having gone there—were you? 15. [They replied: "We were there."
The warding off of dust by my messages.
And you shall perform that mental cultivation; thus, when assistance has been rendered to your body, [it shall be] manifest.
The sense is that it will also serve as an inflamer of passion.
And it has been said: "The body of those devoted to compassion shines through their assistance to others, not by means of sandalwood. [NŚ 63cd]
Of what nature are you?— [you who are] swiftly leaping along the path, the way.
The meaning is "moving swiftly.
In some places, "leaping very swiftly" is also appropriate.
"What shall we say?
He replied: "O traveler, today is the rainy season."
"Your delight in another place"— or rather, "your inclination toward another place"—
let it be released, let it be abandoned.
Or else, in the alternative case: if you do not release her,
then she shall be your wife.
"Either by you or by us—what other person's words shall be spoken? Let them be told! Such is the sense. It consists of eighteen phrases. 8.
O Lord, even the row of swans has now set out through the sky toward Lake Mānasa; and even the thirsty cātaka bird begs for water from the clouds.
The traveler is weary,
and so too is she who belongs to you.
"O Lord! Now, at this very time, during the rainy season.
According to the *Amarakośa* (3.4.24): "etarhi, samprati, idānīm, adhunā, sāmpratam, and tathā" all mean "now. Furthermore, "haṃsānām" means both a row and a line of swans.
In the sky, in the atmosphere,
toward the lake known as Mānasa.
"Prasthitā" means set forth or departed.
Regarding "viyat," the *Amara-kośa* states: "Viyat or viṣṇupada. [1.2.2] But surely, swans [do not fly] upon the earth?
How is it that they do not sport? This has been said:
"Even though there is water everywhere adorned with lotuses, the mind of the swan does not delight [except] in Lake Mānasa. And likewise: "Cāta..."
Someone is thirsty.
"Thirst has arisen for him," thus he is "thirsty."
Furthermore, water is requested and entreated for.
O traveler, that beloved woman is dead.
She, being distressed, begs of you; how can we give her?
Or rather, she is dear to you.
This verse consists of nineteen syllables. Just as the blue grass shines forth exceedingly tender,
so indeed does the *cātaka* bird find pure water.
When the clouds have arisen and the flocks of peacocks are crying out, what pleasure is there?
"O beloved, today without you, this dark-green young grass shines exceedingly; it is most beautiful. And [the word] *nīlam*...
And that is the grass.
That is blue grass.
The *karmadhāraya* has been explained.
Because both [the agent and the object] are primary [in this case], [it is a transitive verb]. [Marginal gloss:
Intoxicating, burning, drying up, and likewise paralyzing.
And the five arrows of Kāma are delusion.
Thus I have remembered it.
[See TKŚ 1.1.40] What kind of grass? Tender and soft. Indeed (*hi*) is used for certainty. *Cātaka* is another name for the *stokaka* bird.
"Samā" means "equal," according to the *Amara-kośa* [2.5.17].
It is stainless (*amalam*), meaning free from impurity (*malavarjitam*); "vāri" means water (*jalam*); it obtains (*vindati*).
It attains [the state of being]. The root *vṛ* means "to cover" (*vṛñ* [DhP X.271]); it covers or conceals the earth, thus it is *vāri*. Likewise, [it is so called] by the clouds (*ambuda*).
By means of clouds.
A flock of crested birds, that is, a multitude of peacocks,
is made to resound, meaning it utters sounds in a particularly intense manner.
[The root] *ṇad* means "to sound" [SV 229,29]. O beloved!
